The slide whistle is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.221.312. It consists of a cylindrical tube with a recorder-like fipple mouthpiece at one end and a piston inside; the player blows while pushing or pulling the piston, so that the pitch rises or falls continuously and produces a glide. Because the air column is open at one end and closed at the other, overblowing reaches the third harmonic. Modern versions are usually of plastic or metal and appeared in nineteenth-century England; folk instruments of a similar kind are found in Africa, Asia, the Pacific and Europe. It is used for animated sound effects, television programmes and special effects in jazz and popular music, and it also appears in opera, ballet and modern classical works, as well as in jug band playing.
滑音哨笛音色清亮透徹，具有獨特的卡通感與戲謔風格，帶有溫暖的木質共鳴。其音域寬廣: The slide whistle's timbre is clear and bright, with a distinctive cartoonish, mocking character and a warm, woody resonance. Its range is wide, and it can produce a continuous change of pitch from low to shrill; it is especially good at smooth glissandi. Because the bore is cylindrical, the instrument tends to overblow into the third harmonic, which gives the upper register a slightly edgy, penetrating timbre. Compared with the veiled refinement of the recorder, the slide whistle sounds lighter and more animated; compared with the saxophone its timbre is brighter and cleaner, with a more direct resonance. The instrument's sound feels intimate, and it often creates humour and a sense of motion in light music, children's music and jazz; its unusual ability to glide continuously makes it the ideal choice for imitating animal calls and sound effects.
現代滑音哨笛主要由塑膠或金屬製成。吹口部分採用類似豎笛的設計，通常由塑膠或硬質橡: The modern slide whistle is mainly made of plastic or metal. The mouthpiece follows a recorder-like design and is usually made of plastic or hard rubber for durability. The body is of transparent or translucent plastic, so that the piston inside can be seen working. The piston itself is usually of metal, smoothly finished so that it slides freely. Folk versions are traditionally made of cane or bamboo. The structure as a whole is simple, and the parts fit closely to keep the instrument airtight.
